title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax
one_liner: A small set of neurons use negative values as a dedicated channel for syntax, separate from semantic meaning.
lead: Modern language models use smooth functions like GELU that let neurons output negative numbers, not just positive ones. Older interpretability work assumed positive outputs carried all the information. This paper shows that negative outputs actually do real work: a tiny fraction of neurons send a specific signal through their negative values, and that signal is what the model uses to track grammar and syntax.

problem.h2: Why did interpretability overlook negative signals?
paras: For decades, the most common neuron activation function was ReLU, which forced all outputs to zero or positive. Since negative values simply did not exist, researchers naturally focused on positive activations (large ones meant the neuron was active, small meant it was not). That habit stuck around even after models switched to GELU and SiLU, which do allow negative values, because interpretability researchers did not yet have a reason to look for negative-value patterns.

A naive approach: assume negative outputs are just noise, either leftover artifacts from the learning process or unused channels. If that were true, you could ignore them or zero them out without losing anything important. But this paper asks: what if they are actually being used for something specific?

callout.b: The shift: negative values might carry real signal, not noise.
callout.html: The paper finds that certain neurons deliberately use their negative outputs to differentiate grammatical structures, separate from semantic meaning.

steps.text: Find neurons whose output distribution is unusual (far from a simple bell curve).
For each neuron, quantify how much signal flows through negative values.
Run grammatical and semantic tests before and after turning off negative values.
Show that damage accumulates as the signal moves deeper through the model.
Prove the effect is specific, not just side effect of ablating random neurons.

paras: The paper modifies how negative activations are treated in a handful of neurons. Specifically, it zeros out only the negative part of the output for these special Wasserstein neurons, while leaving their positive parts and all other neurons untouched.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: what negative channels are doing
hidden.name: Negative-channel syntax load
paras: This paper measures how much of the grammar-detection work flows through the negative output channel of a small, special population of neurons. It is not about overall neuron importance; it is specifically about whether the negative values carry task-critical signal (as opposed to positive values doing all the work).

The paper estimates this quantity by comparing two ablations: zeroing only negative outputs vs. zeroing only positive outputs. If grammar degrades more when negatives are zeroed, that negative channel was carrying syntax information. They also use Wasserstein distance (a mathematical measure of how far a distribution sits from a simple normal curve) to identify which neurons have this special property.

heat.caption: Darker neurons rely more on negative-channel signal for syntax. Marked ones are Wasserstein neurons.

reads.html: A handful of neurons send a message through their negative outputs, like a dedicated wire. Cutting that wire breaks grammar understanding but does not hurt semantic reasoning.

Wasserstein neurons exhibit large deviations from Gaussian output distributions; negative pre-activation ablation (but not positive ablation) causes syntactic task degradation with a double dissociation against non-grammatical benchmarks.

mechanism.h2: Why negative outputs became a syntax channel
paras: During training, the model gradually discovered that it could separate concerns: use one output channel (positive) for what a word means semantically, and a different channel (negative) for how it fits into the sentence structure. This separation is efficient because grammar and semantics are partly independent — a word like 'run' can be a verb or noun depending on context, but the model handles that split in different neurons.

When you zero out the negative values of these Wasserstein neurons, the model loses its dedicated syntax channel. It must now try to pack both grammar and meaning into positive activations alone. The other neurons cannot easily reroute that syntax information because the specialized neurons have already learned to rely on their negative channel; changing them suddenly breaks the downstream reading machinery.

The paper shows this is a real causal effect by comparing to random ablations of other neurons. If you zero out random positive activations across many non-special neurons (damaging them equally badly), grammar performance holds up better, because the model can work around generic damage by rerouting through many paths, but cannot reroute syntax without those specialized negative channels. This proves the syntax channel is not just any part of the network, but specifically the negative values in these Wasserstein neurons.

stages.s: Smooth activation function applied (GELU or SiLU)
Positive values route to semantic layer
Negative values route to syntax layer

math.h2: Measuring the syntax signal in negative activations
math.words: negative-ablation-damage equals (grammar-accuracy-before minus grammar-accuracy-after) minus (semantics-accuracy-before minus semantics-accuracy-after); this difference is large for Wasserstein neurons but small for random neurons
symbols: Grammatical benchmark score after zeroing negatives
Semantic benchmark score after zeroing negatives
Difference between grammar damage and semantic damage
math.note: A large dissociation shows Wasserstein neurons use negatives specifically for syntax, not as a side effect.

bars.h2: Grammar vs. semantics under different ablations

charts.title: Wasserstein negative ablation
charts.note: Syntax crashes; semantics barely dents. This is the smoking gun.

charts.title: Random neuron ablation (perplexity-matched control)
charts.note: Random ablation hurts semantics more, proving negatives in Wasserstein neurons specialize in syntax.

items.b: Negative activations are not always used.
items.html: This signal only exists in a tiny population of Wasserstein neurons. Most neurons do not split syntax and semantics into different polarity channels. The discovery is specific, not universal.

Models with ReLU do not allow negative outputs, so this syntax channel cannot exist, because the model has no way to send signals through negative values. Smooth activations like GELU and SiLU are required for this division of labor to emerge.
Small ablations of negatives in one layer only slightly degrade grammar; but the same ablation in every layer adds up to major failure. The effect is distributed across depth, not localized.

The paper controls for perplexity (total model confusion) and shows random ablations have different effects. The sign-specific targeting of Wasserstein negative activations is causal, not coincidental.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small language model (a few million parameters) with a smooth activation and train it on a task with grammar + semantics (e.g., predicting the next word in grammatically varied sentences). Measure Wasserstein distance for each neuron. Identify the high-Wasserstein ones. For those neurons only, zero out negative pre-activations and measure grammar accuracy on a held-out grammatical benchmark (BLiMP-style) and a semantic benchmark (word-sense or factual). Compare to zeroing positive pre-activations (or random neuron negatives) to confirm the double dissociation.
demo.closing: If the dissociation is large (>5x) for Wasserstein neurons and near 1.0 for random neurons, the demo proves syntax and semantics are routed through different polarity channels in these special neurons.
